children: The Florida Bar has rejected an ethics complaint filed by 128 former judges accusing the U.S. Department of Homeland Security’s top lawyer of violating professional conduct rules by posting on social media about what he called the “worst of the worst” judges who have ruled against the Trump administration.
A group of former judges led by former Florida Supreme Court Chief Justice Peggy Quince filed the
on August 18 against James Percival, saying the DHS general counsel's social media posts impugned the integrity of four sitting judges and exposed them to potential threats.
, an official with the state bar in Florida, where Percival is licensed, said it "does not investigate or prosecute sitting officers appointed under the U.S. Constitution while they are in office."

"Such proceedings by The Florida Bar, as an arm of the Florida Supreme Court, could encroach on the authority of the federal government concerning these officials and the exercise of their duties," wrote bar counsel Christopher Wackes.
As a result, the matter was closed, with Wackes informing Quince that she could refile the complaint once Percival no longer serves in office.

Percival, in a social media post on Monday, highlighted the end of the Florida Bar case with a picture of his face smiling and superimposed onto the body of the character Gandalf from "The Lord of the Rings."

A spokesperson for Democracy Defenders Fund, a liberal legal group that filed the judges' complaint alongside the organization Lawyers Defending American Democracy, did not respond to a request for comment on Tuesday.

Percival faced criticism from judges and others in the legal community over a series of posts he made on the social media platform X beginning in mid-July featuring what he called the “Worst of the Worst, District Judge Edition."

The title was a play on DHS' practice of making announcements highlighting the "worst of the worst" individuals who have been arrested or deported during President Donald Trump's immigration crackdown.

Among the judges who became a focus of Percival's posts were U.S. District Judge Matthew Kennelly in Chicago and U.S. District Judges Patti Saris, Brian Murphy and Allison Burroughs in Boston, appointees of Democratic presidents who were weighing bids to block DHS from ending temporary protected status for non-citizens from four countries.

The judges ultimately allowed TPS to end in those four countries, rejecting last-minute bids to maintain the migrants' protected status after the U.S. Supreme Court allowed TPS to end for Haitians and Syrians.
